Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette: Maria is a 19-year-old Latin American woman who has recently sought help for symptoms that have been disrupting her life. As a train conductor in a busy urban area, Maria’s work and daily environment are integral to understanding the development of her PTSD symptoms. Maria witnessed domestic violence growing up, an event that still haunts her today. The specific triggers she experiences—darkness, loud noises, and the sensation of her heart racing—are directly linked to the night when the incident occurred. The room was dark, her heart pounding with fear as she listened to the escalating sounds from another part of the house. These triggers often bring back vivid memories of that night, making it feel like the event is happening all over again. When Maria hears a loud noise on her commute home or sees dark areas in the train station at night, she immediately relives those terrifying moments. The memory’s intensity and confusion about the sequence of events further exacerbate her distress. Maria had come to believe that she couldn’t stop bad things from happening, which added to her sense of helplessness. She was certain that if she had done something differently, maybe protected others better, the outcome would have been different. This self-blame has made it even harder for her to process and move past the traumatic memories. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Maria has developed several maladaptive strategies. She keeps herself incredibly busy at work, often working extra shifts and pushing herself beyond what is comfortable. She also engages in counterfactual thinking, frequently pondering how life would have been different if she had not witnessed the violence. Additionally, she tends to undereat, avoiding food as a way of coping with her anxiety. The memories that feel so present exacerbate Maria’s sense of threat and vigilance. At night, when it feels hardest for her to find safety, she checks door locks repeatedly and finds herself on high alert for any unexpected sounds. This heightened state of alertness further reinforces her negative appraisals and makes the memory feel even more intense. The cycle is self-reinforcing: as Maria’s triggers bring back vivid memories, they feed into her sense of threat and helplessness. These feelings drive her to engage in maladaptive coping strategies like busyness and undereating, which in turn keep the memory alive and potent. The memory itself intensifies her negative appraisals and exacerbates her fear responses. This cycle has led to tangible changes in Maria’s life. Her work as a train conductor has become increasingly challenging; she struggles to focus during shifts and often avoids certain parts of her route due to dark spaces or loud noises. Her relationships have also suffered, with friends noticing that she seems distant and preoccupied. What finally brought Maria to seek help was the realization that her coping mechanisms were no longer working—she felt more trapped by these memories than ever before. She is most afraid of losing control completely and is hoping for a way to regain some sense of safety and normalcy in her life. Maria’s story illustrates how her triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat perceptions, memory disturbances, and negative appraisals have interwoven into a complex and self-perpetuating cycle. Each element feeds into the next, creating a web of distress that has significantly impacted her daily functioning and well-being.
